memoryText: O Israel, hope in the LORD! For with the LORD there is steadfast love, and with him is plentiful redemption.
readingInstruction: Today there is no new reading. This week you finished the story of Samson, sang two psalms of waiting and hope, walked through the terrible last chapters of Judges, and began the book of Ruth. Rest today in the single hope that runs through it all: with the LORD there is steadfast love and plentiful redemption.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Psalm 130:7 turns the week’s darkness into hope. After the idols of Micah and the horrors of Gibeah, here is the word that tells us why God’s people can keep going.

“O Israel, hope in the LORD!” This is a command and an invitation. The psalmist has been in the depths and has found his way up. Now he turns to the whole people and tells them to hope. Hope is not a feeling that arrives on its own. It is a decision to trust the one who has spoken.

“For with the LORD there is steadfast love.” The Hebrew word is hesed, the covenant love that does not let go. It is the love Ruth showed to Naomi and the love God shows to his people. It does not depend on their performance. It is committed to them.

“And with him is plentiful redemption.” The word “plentiful” is a reminder that God’s supply is greater than our need. If your sin is great, his redemption is greater. The judges failed, and the people failed, but the redemption did not run out.

For the Christian, this verse points to Christ. “In him we have redemption through his blood” (Ephesians 1:7). The plentiful redemption has a name. Say the verse aloud, and carry it into any moment this week when you feel the weight of sin or the weariness of waiting. Hope in the LORD.
weekInReview:
This week you saw both the lowest point of Israel’s history and the first light of recovery. You finished Samson’s story, with Delilah’s betrayal, the loss of his strength, and his last prayer. You sang Psalm 130, out of the depths, and Psalm 40, the testimony of one lifted from the pit. You read the stories of Micah’s private idol and the Danites’ theft, and you read the horror of Gibeah and the civil war that followed, ending with the line that explains it all: “In those days there was no king in Israel.” Then you turned to Ruth. You met a Moabite widow who clung to her mother-in-law and her mother-in-law’s God, a bitter Naomi who came home empty, and a generous Boaz in the barley field. The word “redeemer” appeared.

The week held a clear contrast: the nation of Israel did what was right in its own eyes, and a single woman chose to take refuge under the wings of the LORD.
reflectionQuestions: Where do you see yourself in the cycle of Judges this week? Think about the pattern: forgetting God, hitting trouble, crying out, being rescued, and drifting again. Where are you in that cycle right now? What would it look like to break the pattern with a deeper, daily dependence on God?

How does the “plentiful redemption” of Psalm 130 find its fullest meaning in Jesus? Judges ends with a nation that needs a true king and a redeemer. Ruth introduces a kinsman-redeemer who will rescue a family. How does Christ, the greater king and the greater redeemer, answer what Judges leaves unresolved? What does it mean for you that your sin is not too big for his redemption?

Who is your “Ruth” or “Naomi”? Think about the people who have shown steadfast loyalty to you, and the people who need it from you. Is there a person in your life who is bitter, empty, or alone? What is one way you could stay with them this coming week?
prayerPrompts: Thank God for his steadfast love and plentiful redemption.
Thank him that he never stopped working in the dark days.
